title: Berkshire Hathaway Energy — Technology Study Guide

sections.title: The PPA-side utility: a fourth answer to one question
ps: The corpus now holds four answers to how a regulated utility serves a gigawatt of new load without sending the bill to everyone else. Dominion's is a rate class with a {{minimum demand charge}}. DTE's is a {{special contract}} in which the customer pays for utility-owned batteries. WEC's is a subscription to named plants at a fixed return. Berkshire Hathaway Energy's lead utility, NV Energy, gives the fourth: contract for almost every new resource under a {{PPA}}, keep only the firm gas in {{rate base}}, and write a bilateral service agreement whose commercial numbers the regulator fills in.

The scale is the reason it matters. NV Energy's 2026 {{IRP}} asks the Nevada {{public utility commission}} to approve 23 power purchase agreements — about 4,370 MW of paired solar, 180 MW of geothermal and 5,405 MW of battery output by 2031 — plus 1,223 MW of utility-owned gas turbines at Fort Churchill for 2030 to 2032, against about 22,000 MW of data-center inquiries and a system whose two utilities peaked at about 8,200 MW in 2025. The parent's rule, stated by Berkshire's CEO in September 2026, is that hyperscalers will be served 'if there was no impact to the rates'.

This guide teaches what a high-school-STEM reader needs to follow that: where the equipment decision goes when a plan is bought by contract; the difference between paying for wires and paying for generation; what a large-load service agreement contains and why its percentages were left blank; why a utility would sue its own largest prospective customer over which forum decides; how {{wildfire liability}} rather than load became the binding constraint on a six-state utility; and what a grid without a {{capacity market}} does instead.

sections.title: Wires versus generation: Rule 9 and the LLESA
ps: **Paying for wires.** Under NV Energy's Rule 9, a large customer signs a {{line-extension agreement}}: it advances the cost of the distribution and transmission facilities built to reach it and commits to minimum usage. About 6 GW of these were signed against about 22 GW of inquiries. But the utility's own words are that they 'do not address generation' — the wires arrive and there is nothing to send down them.

**Paying for generation.** The 2026 IRP therefore files a form {{large-load electric service agreement}} for any accelerated load of 25 MW or more — the lowest threshold in this corpus. It adds a contracted maximum demand and ramp schedule, minimum billing for demand and energy, a customer-specific generation charge recovered from the customer before any plant enters rate base, a termination payment, and customer security under objective credit standards. Where the other three models make the customer pay through a tariff or a subscription, this one charges for the plant up front, as a contribution.

**Why the split matters to a seller.** The wires charge decides when a campus is energized; the generation charge decides whether the utility's plan — the batteries and turbines above — gets built for it. A customer that has paid for wires but not for generation is exactly the customer that buys its own bridging plants (below).

sections.title: A utility sues its customer: the forum question
ps: In June 2024 Tract's Reno Power signed agreements with NV Energy for its Storey County technology parks. On June 16, 2026 Tract demanded private arbitration under them. On July 24 the utility sued Tract Capital Management in Washoe County — not to change a price, but to keep three questions in front of the commission rather than an arbitrator: whether the supply is adequate, who pays for the network, and how Tract's load is treated in the resource plan. NV Energy's phrase was that Tract wants it 'to reserve and provide enormous amounts of power for Tract's private development while shifting the infrastructure and energy costs to Nevada families'. Tract's was that the suit is 'a public relations blitz', that it has spent more than $127M and committed about $1B of upgrades.

The arithmetic explains the forum fight. The utility says Tract plans 'at least five data centers with a combined load of nearly 5.5 GW' — two-thirds of a system that peaked at about 8,200 MW. A regulator owes a duty to every customer and can weigh {{cross-subsidy}}; an arbitrator is bound to the two parties in front of it. The question of who decides is therefore the question of whether the other 1.5 million customers are in the room.

The customer's answer was to stop waiting. Fleet's project companies applied in April 2026 for temporary gas plants — 218 MW at Peru Ridge and 144 MW at South Valley, about 90 LNG containerized {{reciprocating engine}}s and 136 CNG units — to run two to three years until utility service arrives. Storey County approved them in July; the commission conditionally approved them on September 17, 2026, the same day the governor's executive order gave it the mandate the utility's suit presupposes. For a seller of engines, turbines and switchgear the lesson is that {{behind-the-meter}} bridging generation is now a permitted product in Nevada precisely because the utility's plan could not deliver in time.

sections.title: Wildfire liability: the constraint that is not load
ps: **The number.** PacifiCorp — the group's six-state western utility — has accrued $2.85B of probable {{wildfire liability}} through mid-2026 and paid $2.3B; class verdicts of about $1.2B were reversed and sent back in April 2026 and the Oregon Supreme Court hears the case on November 3, 2026, with 'reasonably possible' further material losses. A utility's ability to build is its ability to borrow, and an unbounded tort liability sits on the same balance sheet as the plan.

**What it costs.** S&P put PacifiCorp on watch for junk in March 2026 after two verdicts; a $2.55B letter-of-credit facility, a $575M federal settlement and a $150M plaintiff settlement followed; and the sale of the Washington service area to Portland General ($1.9B, closing 2027), the Oregon co-op sales and a {{sale-leaseback}} of the Boardman-to-Hemingway line (about $1.1B) are modeled as liquidity for the damages case. The three-year plan spends $1.5B on wildfire prevention and $0.1B on new wind.

**What it does to the data-center book.** In Oregon more than 7,000 MW is pursued, 784 MW is under contract, negotiations have 'stalled' under the 2025 large-load statute, and Amazon has complained to the regulator that the utility failed to serve it. In Utah a first contract under the 2025 large-load law is worth 'nearly $1 billion' of net benefits. The 2025 IRP Update added 2,223 MW of gas proxies and 4,677 MW of storage proxies by 2045 — a plan with no procurement door open in 2026. State tort law — Utah's caps, Wyoming's zero noneconomic liability, Oregon's defeated bills — now decides part of who gets served.

sections.title: Markets without an auction: EDAM, WEIM and the IRP as the reliability rule
ps: Exelon's customers in PJM pay a {{capacity market}} price for generators to exist. BHE's western utilities do not: there is no capacity auction west of the Rockies outside California, so {{resource adequacy}} is a planning duty — NV Energy's 2026 IRP targets an open position of no more than 500 MW short by 2031, and the Western Resource Adequacy Program sits in PacifiCorp's plan as a regional check. What the West has instead is an {{energy imbalance market}}: PacifiCorp launched in CAISO's Extended Day-Ahead Market on May 1, 2026 as the first western utility, NV Energy trades in the real-time market, and both save money by balancing across a footprint rather than alone. Nobody pays them for capacity.

The consequence for the data-center book is that firm capacity is whatever the IRP builds or contracts, on the IRP's timetable. NV Energy's earliest new turbine is 2029–2030; the plan says 'total new thermal may exceed 3 GW in next decade'. That gap between a customer's 2027 energization date and the utility's first turbine is the space Tract's bridging plants occupy — and the reason a Nevada regulator approved gas generation built by a data-center developer.

MidAmerican, the group's Iowa utility, sits in {{MISO}} and answers large load with a contract rather than a market: the {{load commitment agreement}} — a binding ramp, a minimum monthly charge payable for ten years regardless of usage, exit penalties and customer funding of every substation and line. The forecast counts only signed ones; data centers are about 8 percent of Iowa peak; there is no tariff docket and no litigation. It is the quietest large-load franchise in the corpus because it is a contract that predates the tariff wave.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **Treating the 5.4 GW as a utility purchase order.** It is 23 PPAs; the utility buys none of the hardware. The seller's counterparties are the developers.
**Reading the LLESA as a tariff with rates.** It is a form whose percentages the customers reserved for the commission; the numbers do not exist yet.
**Calling the Tract case a price dispute.** It is a forum dispute — regulator or arbitrator — over supply adequacy and cost allocation.
**Assuming a capacity market.** The West has imbalance markets and planning duties; nobody is paid to exist, so the IRP's turbine date is the firm-capacity date.
**Reading BHE's 11 GW as NV Energy's.** It is the group figure across three utilities; NV Energy's own 2030 forecast is 3.6 GW of peak.
**Forgetting the balance sheet.** PacifiCorp's wildfire accrual, not its load forecast, decides what it can build; the Oregon Supreme Court argument is November 3, 2026.

cards.q: In NV Energy's 2026 plan, who chooses the battery cells and integrator for the 5,405 MW of new storage?
cards.a: The developers who hold the 23 power purchase agreements — chosen at bid stage in the 2024 all-source RFP; the utility owns only Reid Gardner (BYD cells, Energy Vault EPC) and Sierra Solar.

cards.q: What does a Rule 9 line-extension agreement pay for, and what does it not?
cards.a: The distribution and transmission built to reach the customer, with a minimum-usage commitment — not generation; about 6 GW were signed against 22 GW of inquiries.

cards.q: What does the form LLESA add, and at what threshold?
cards.a: A maximum demand and ramp, minimum billing for demand and energy, a customer-specific generation charge recovered before rate base, a termination payment and customer security — for accelerated loads of 25 MW or more, the lowest threshold in the corpus.

cards.q: Who sets the LLESA's minimum-bill percentages, generation charge and security?
cards.a: The Nevada commission — all four filing customers reserved them in Exhibit G; the governor's September 2026 order directs the PUCN to set an instrument ensuring 'no burden on other ratepayers'.

cards.q: What is NV Energy's suit against Tract actually about?
cards.a: The forum: keeping supply adequacy, cost allocation and resource-plan treatment of Tract's ~5.5 GW before the regulator rather than the private arbitrator Tract demanded in June 2026.

cards.q: What did the PUCN approve on September 17, 2026, and why does it matter to an equipment seller?
cards.a: Tract/Fleet's 362 MW of temporary gas plants (218 + 144 MW) to run two to three years until utility service — behind-the-meter bridging generation is now a permitted product because the plan could not deliver in time.

cards.q: Why does PacifiCorp spend more on wildfire prevention than on new generation?
cards.a: $2.85B of accrued wildfire losses, a junk watch and a $2.55B letter-of-credit facility make the balance sheet the constraint; the plan is liquidity first, and Oregon negotiations have stalled.

cards.q: How is reliability assured in the West without a capacity market?
cards.a: By the integrated resource plan — NV Energy targets an open position of no more than 500 MW short by 2031 — while imbalance markets (EDAM, WEIM) trade energy but pay nobody for capacity.

cards.q: What is MidAmerican's load commitment agreement?
cards.a: A binding ramp, a minimum monthly charge payable for ten years regardless of usage, exit penalties and customer funding of all incremental T&D — a contract rather than a tariff, so the forecast counts only signed ones.

cards.q: What is the parent's rule for serving hyperscalers?
cards.a: Serve them 'if there was no impact to the rates' — which a fixed-price PPA satisfies visibly and a nonregulated behind-the-meter affiliate satisfies by construction.

items.q: A storage integrator wants its product in NV Energy's 2026 battery build. Who is the buyer it must win?
c: The developers behind the 23 PPAs, at bid stage — the utility buys none of the 5,405 MW
items.why: The plan is 'more than 5,400 MW of battery storage through power purchase agreements'; only Reid Gardner and Sierra Solar are owned, and both are contracted.

items.q: A data center has signed a Rule 9 agreement and paid for its substation and lines. What has it not yet secured?
c: Generation — Rule 9 'does not address generation'; that is what the LLESA's customer-specific generation charge is for
items.why: Wires and generation are separate instruments in Nevada.

items.q: Why did NV Energy sue Tract rather than arbitrate?
c: To keep supply adequacy, cost allocation and resource-plan treatment before a regulator with a duty to all customers, instead of an arbitrator bound to two parties
items.why: The suit is about which forum decides; the utility calls Tract's plan a cost shift to 'Nevada families'.

items.q: Which statement about the PUCN's September 17, 2026 approval is correct?
c: It approved NV Energy's Fort Churchill turbines
It conditionally approved Tract/Fleet's 362 MW of temporary gas plants — the customer's bridge while utility service is built
items.why: The IRP decision is due December 2; the executive order the same day instructs the PUCN on the cost-of-service instrument.

items.q: Why does a wildfire verdict in Oregon affect whether a Utah data center is served?
c: One balance sheet, one credit rating and one liquidity plan serve six states; the accrued liability sets the cost of every dollar borrowed to build
items.why: $2.85B accrued, a junk watch in March 2026, and a plan that spends $1.5B on wildfire against $0.1B on new generation.

items.q: A hyperscaler wants firm capacity in Nevada in 2028. Which route is NOT available?
c: An LLESA subscribing to NV Energy's owned Valmy peakers and Fort Churchill turbines as they arrive
A Clean Transition Tariff resource it pays for
Its own permitted bridging generation, as Tract did
Buying capacity in a western capacity auction
items.why: There is no capacity market in the West; resource adequacy is an IRP duty and imbalance markets trade energy only.
